research_question: Was Spinosaurus an aquatic pursuit predator, and how strong is the evidence?

stance_values.aquatic: argues Spinosaurus (or spinosaurids) were aquatic / semi-aquatic swimmers or divers that foraged underwater
stance_values.wading: argues against aquatic pursuit/diving; favours a shoreline, wading, bipedal ambush ('heron-like') predator
stance_values.mixed: evidence or coverage that cuts both ways, or supports a fish diet without deciding between pursuit and wading
stance_values.background: anatomy, taxonomy, discovery history or environment without taking a side on the ecology question
stance_values.tangential: related spinosaurid work that a good search agent should rank low for this question

relation_values.rebuts: argues against the target's central conclusion
relation_values.supports: presents new evidence or argument in favour of the target's conclusion
relation_values.reports_on: journalism or press release about the target
relation_values.summarizes: restates the target's evidence (useful stand-in when the target is unavailable)

key_claims: A new neotype skeleton shows Spinosaurus had retracted nares, a reduced pelvis and hindlimbs, dense long bones lacking open medullary cavities, and flat-bottomed pedal unguals, all interpreted as semiaquatic adaptations.
Its centre of mass lay well forward of the hips, implying it was likely quadrupedal on land and spent much of its time foraging in water.
A nearly complete tail from the neotype has very tall neural spines and elongate chevrons that form a large, flexible, fin-like tail unique among dinosaurs.
Robotic flapping experiments show this tail produces far more thrust, more efficiently, than the tails of terrestrial theropods, supporting tail-propelled swimming in a largely aquatic predator.

Bone compactness of femora and dorsal ribs, analysed with phylogenetic flexible discriminant analysis across a large amniote sample, classifies Spinosaurus and Baryonyx as subaqueous foragers (divers).
Suchomimus is classified as non-diving, implying ecological diversity within Spinosauridae.
Myhrvold et al.'s criticisms (selective bone sampling, inadequate statistics, inaccurate ecological categories) misrepresent the original analyses as qualitative interpretations of plots.
Re-analyses using the original datasets plus Myhrvold et al.'s new data still recover Spinosaurus and Baryonyx as subaqueous foragers and Suchomimus as non-diving.
The inference that spinosaurids were 'subaqueous foragers' rests on selectively sampled bone cross-sections and problematic statistical inference.
Bone compactness data as analysed by Fabbri et al. cannot reliably establish diving behaviour in Spinosaurus or Baryonyx.
Bone compactness varies strongly along a bone and between sections, and Fabbri et al.'s dataset contains measurement and categorisation errors.
pFDA classifications of lifestyle from bone compactness are unreliable for these taxa, so the data do not support inferring diving or an aquatic habit for spinosaurids.
CT-based digital flesh models show Spinosaurus would have been unstable floating at the surface and too buoyant to dive, and its tail and body make it a slow, inefficient swimmer.

Its centre of mass lay over the hind feet, so it was a capable biped on land, best interpreted as a semiaquatic bipedal ambush piscivore of shorelines and shallow water rather than an aquatic pursuit predator.
3D digital models place Spinosaurus's centre of mass close to the hips, consistent with bipedality rather than the anterior position claimed for the neotype reconstruction.
A floating Spinosaurus would have been buoyant and laterally unstable, prone to tipping onto its side, which argues against a semi-aquatic, diving lifestyle.
A review of anatomical, ecological and taphonomic evidence finds Spinosaurus poorly suited to being an aquatic pursuit predator.
Spinosaurus is best interpreted as a shoreline generalist that waded and hunted fish and other prey from the water's edge, in a heron-like or stork-like way.
The newly described swim tail, considered with the body it propelled and compared using Reynolds numbers, suggests Spinosaurus was a specialised deep-water predator.
The dorsal sail and head shape can be interpreted as hydrodynamic adaptations for underwater manoeuvring and prey capture.

Rather than thermoregulation, fat storage or display, the dorsal sail of a semiaquatic Spinosaurus could have worked underwater, improving manoeuvrability and acting as a hydrodynamic fulcrum for powerful neck and tail strikes, as in sailfish or thresher sharks.
The sail may also have been used as a screen to herd or encircle prey underwater.
A large spinosaurine tibia from the Romualdo Formation of Brazil is osteosclerotic and has a reduced fibular crest, features otherwise seen only in Spinosaurus aegyptiacus.
High bone compactness, a correlate of semi-aquatic habits, was already present in Brazilian spinosaurines millions of years before the Moroccan Spinosaurus.
Spinosaurid jaws converge with those of pike conger eels: a compressed, elongate rostrum, a terminal rosette of enlarged teeth, and a notch behind it.

This jaw design, together with integumentary mechanoreceptors in the snout, is interpreted as an adaptation for seizing elusive prey in low-light aquatic environments, supporting a semi-aquatic lifestyle.
Oxygen isotope compositions of spinosaurid tooth phosphate resemble those of co-occurring crocodilians and turtles more than those of other theropods.
This indicates spinosaurids spent much of their time in water, i.e. had semi-aquatic habits.
The abundance and preservation of Spinosaurus remains in the Kem Kem fluvial deposits, relative to other theropods, is argued to reflect an animal that lived predominantly in water.
Juvenile spinosaurine remains of various sizes are relatively common in the Kem Kem beds, suggesting juveniles occupied the same semiaquatic, piscivorous niche as adults in deltaic habitats.
The absence of very small (<2 m) individuals may reflect taphonomic bias or that the earliest ontogenetic stages lived in different environments.
Spinosaurids from Niger and Morocco have the most negative tooth-enamel calcium isotope values of all predators sampled.

This indicates niche partitioning in which spinosaurids foraged on aquatic resources while abelisaurids and carcharodontosaurids relied on terrestrial prey; it shows diet, not whether prey was caught by swimming or wading.
Calcium isotope work shows Spinosaurus was strongly depleted in heavy calcium, best explained by a predominantly fish diet.
The isotope researcher interviewed does not think Spinosaurus was fully aquatic: isotopes constrain its food source, not whether it swam or waded.
In multivariate skull-shape space, spinosaurids including Spinosaurus plot away from other theropods and close to both marine taxa and wading birds.
Skull shape separates taxa by aquatic versus terrestrial food rather than cleanly by terrestrial, semi-aquatic or aquatic habitat, so skull shape alone cannot settle Spinosaurus's habitat.
Beam-theory analysis of CT-derived rostra compares Baryonyx and Spinosaurus with gharial, slender-snouted crocodile and alligator for resistance to bending and torsion.
The biomechanics suggest spinosaurs were not obligate piscivores, with diet depending on individual body size.
The endocranium and inner ear of Irritator indicate fast, well-controlled pitch-down head movements and a habitually down-angled snout.
These features are interpreted as potential adaptations for snapping at small, agile prey such as fish (comparative evidence from another spinosaurid), not as evidence of swimming.
Lines of von Ebner in spinosaurid teeth from Morocco give tooth formation times of up to about 271 days and replacement rates of about 59-68 days, faster than in other large theropods.
Fast replacement plus many teeth per jaw may help explain the abundance of spinosaur teeth in the Kem Kem, an alternative to purely ecological explanations.
A tiny pedal ungual from the Kem Kem beds belongs to the smallest known Spinosaurus individual, an early juvenile.
It is proportionally identical to the corresponding ungual of the neotype partial skeleton, supporting referral of that skeleton to Spinosaurus.
The spinosaurid quadrate and jaw joint allowed the lower jaw rami to spread laterally on opening, widening the pharynx to swallow large prey.
Quadrate morphology indicates that Spinosaurus and a second spinosaurine taxon were present in the Cenomanian of North Africa.
Two new baryonychine spinosaurids, Ceratosuchops inferodios and Riparovenator milnerae, are described from the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, UK.
Phylogenetic analysis suggests a European origin for Spinosauridae and its major subclades.
Iberospinus natarioi is named as a new spinosaurid theropod from the Barremian of Cabo Espichel, Portugal.
The description informs spinosaurid diversity and phylogeny on the Iberian Peninsula.
Protathlitis cinctorrensis is named as a new baryonychine spinosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) of Cinctorres, Spain.
The find adds to the Iberian record of spinosaurid diversity and is used to discuss spinosaurid biogeography.

Spinosaurus mirabilis, a new species with a scimitar-shaped cranial crest, is described from the central Sahara, where it was found alongside long-necked sauropods in a riparian (river-margin) habitat.
Spinosaurid evolution is divided into three discrete phases; the describers, led by the main proponent of the wading model, nicknamed the species the 'hell heron'.
Spinosaurus aegyptiacus was described by Ernst Stromer in 1915 from Egypt; the holotype was destroyed in 1944 and later work relies on Moroccan Kem Kem material, including a 2014 neotype.
The article summarises the ongoing debate between the aquatic/semi-aquatic hypotheses (2014, 2020, 2022 bone density) and the wading/shoreline interpretation (2018, 2021, 2022, 2024).
Spinosauridae is a family of Cretaceous theropods with long, crocodile-like snouts and conical teeth, usually divided into Baryonychinae and Spinosaurinae.
The family is widely associated with fish-eating and with waterside or semi-aquatic habits, with the degree of aquatic adaptation debated.
Ernst Stromer was the German palaeontologist who described Spinosaurus aegyptiacus from Egyptian material collected in the early 20th century.
On 25 April 1944 an RAF bombing raid on Munich destroyed most of his Egyptian specimens on display in the Bavarian State Collection of Palaeontology, including the only known Spinosaurus skeleton.

Spinosaurus mirabilis is a second Spinosaurus species named in 2026 from the Cenomanian Farak Formation of Niger, distinguished by an enlarged nasal-prefrontal crest and nicknamed 'hell heron' by its describers.
Its remains come from a fluvial system where it coexisted with Carcharodontosaurus, sauropods and crocodylomorphs.
The Kem Kem Group of eastern Morocco is a mid-Cretaceous (Cenomanian) fluvial and deltaic sequence with an abundant fossil record of fish, crocodyliforms, pterosaurs and large predatory dinosaurs.
It is the source of most Moroccan Spinosaurus material and provides the environmental context for the ecology debate.
Baryonyx walkeri, from the Early Cretaceous of England, was the first spinosaurid known from a substantial skeleton.
Its preserved stomach contents include fish scales and bones of a juvenile ornithopod, evidence that spinosaurids ate fish but were not exclusively piscivorous (comparative evidence).
Suchomimus tenerensis is a large baryonychine spinosaurid from the Early Cretaceous Elrhaz Formation of Niger with a long, crocodile-like snout and fish-eating adaptations.
It is a frequent comparison taxon for Spinosaurus (e.g. in buoyancy and bone-density studies), but the article itself does not argue for either side of the aquatic debate.
Journalistic coverage of the 2020 tail discovery presenting Spinosaurus as the first known swimming dinosaur with a fin-like, propulsive tail.

Harvard co-authors Stephanie Pierce and George Lauder built robotic tail models showing that the large, flexible tail fin would have given Spinosaurus strong propulsive thrust in water, similar to a salamander or crocodile tail.
University press release reporting new evidence that Spinosaurus was too land-adapted to function even as a slow underwater predator, and was instead a shoreline/wading hunter.

University press release covering two studies that continue the debate over whether Spinosaurus pursued prey underwater or hunted along the shoreline: the 2024 critique of bone-density inference and the bone-density authors' reply.

Feature article (prompted by Spinosaurus swimming in Jurassic World Rebirth) explaining that the hypothesis that Spinosaurus lived mostly submerged remains highly controversial, and laying out evidence on both sides.
